chapterTitle: Crafting Objects Flexibly: Factory Method and Abstract Factory Patterns
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 15-minute interactive code demo. Begin by explaining the problem of tightly coupled object creation using a simple `if-else` example for creating different `Car` types. Then, refactor this into a Factory Method pattern, showing how a `CarFactory` can be subclassed to produce `Sedan`, `SUV`, or `SportsCar` objects. Next, introduce the Abstract Factory by extending the example to create `Engine` and `Tire` families for `LuxuryCarFactory` and `EconomyCarFactory`, demonstrating how they ensure consistent product families. Include live coding, step-by-step explanations, and visual highlighting of interfaces and concrete implementations. End with a mini-quiz comparing the applicability of Factory Method vs. Abstract Factory.

screens.title: Crafting Objects Flexibly
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we explore two creational patterns that free client code from knowing how objects are created. You will learn why encapsulating creation matters, how the Factory Method lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate, and how the Abstract Factory groups related products into compatible families. To ground this, we'll use a cross-platform UI example — think buttons and checkboxes that must behave consistently on Windows or Mac — and a small hands-on document-conversion activity. This matters because hard-coded instantiation with branching logic tightly couples clients to concrete classes and violates the Open/Closed Principle. A simple if-else that returns different button classes becomes a maintenance burden as platforms or product types grow. Throughout the lesson you will see concrete code examples that show the abstract interfaces, concrete products, and factory classes. You'll also compare Factory Method to a simple factory and learn the trade-off: Factory Method favors extensibility via inheritance, while Abstract Factory favors consistent product families. By the end, you should be able to choose the right pattern for single-product creation or for families of related products, and implement a clean factory structure in your codebase. Reflect: which part of your recent project would benefit from hiding creation details behind a factory?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Crafting Objects Flexibly
Crafting Objects Flexibly
Factory Method and Abstract Factory patterns for decoupled creation and consistent product families.
In this lesson you will understand intent, structure, and trade-offs, and implement examples for UI and document conversion.
Why this matters
When client code directly instantiates concrete classes, every change ripples across the codebase. Encapsulating creation keeps code open for extension and closed for modification.
Factory Method
Subclasses decide which product to create; use for single product variants.
Abstract Factory
Creates families of related products so components remain compatible.
Hands-on
Implement a document converter using the Factory Method starter code.
Visual concept
Abstract Factory
Returns a set of related products that work together.
Factory Method
Subclasses implement a creation method for a product.
Open/Closed
Add new variants without changing clients.
Explore Key Topics
Factory Method: defer instantiation to subclasses. Abstract Factory: produce families like buttons and checkboxes. Hands-on Activity: finish the document converter starter code to see the pattern in action.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus your practice on the problem and the two patterns that solve it. First, you will identify the core problem Creational Patterns address: decoupling object creation from client code so implementations can change without breaking clients. Second, you will explain the intent, structure, and application of the Factory Method pattern, including how a creator interface and concrete creators collaborate. Third, you will implement Factory Method in a small example, enabling different concrete products to be made by subclasses. Fourth, you will distinguish Factory Method from a simple factory, understanding that Factory Method uses inheritance to delegate creation and supports extensibility without modifying client code. Each objective includes a short practical mnemonic or micro-check to help you verify competency. For example, when you inspect client code, you should be able to point to a factory method and explain which subclass controls the concrete type. That skill lets you refactor an if-else chain into a factory structure safely. Keep these objectives in mind as we move into code and patterns; they map directly to the hands-on activity and assessment items that follow.

screens.title: The Creational Problem: Why Encapsulate Creation?
screens.narratorSegment: Creational patterns address a simple but pervasive problem: client code depends on concrete classes when it instantiates objects directly. When clients perform branching logic to choose which class to construct, any change to creation details or any new variant forces edits in many places. Encapsulating creation means moving instantiation behind an abstract interface so clients ask for a product and don't know, nor need to know, the concrete class. Concretely, imagine UI code that needs platform-specific buttons. If you scatter conditionals that say "if platform is Windows, new WindowsButton; else if Mac, new MacButton", every new platform or change to construction logic requires touching those conditionals. Encapsulate creation by introducing a creator with a factory method and concrete factories that return the platform-specific button. A common misconception is that encapsulating creation adds unnecessary indirection; in truth, the indirection is an investment in stability and extension. Another misconception is to confuse this with just moving conditionals into a single helper function; that simple factory centralizes branching but still couples the helper and consumers differently than Factory Method, which delegates creation to subclasses. Key takeaway: hide construction behind an abstract contract so client code depends only on interfaces, enabling new variants without editing clients. Ask yourself: when you add a new product in your codebase, do you have to change many client files?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Encapsulate object creation to prevent client code from depending on concrete constructors and to follow the Open/Closed Principle.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › The Creational Problem
Core Concept
Why encapsulate creation?
When clients construct concrete classes directly, changes to creation logic force widespread edits. Encapsulation localizes creation and protects clients.
Concrete example
Cross-platform UI code that instantiates WindowsButton or MacButton using conditionals will need edits for new platforms. Encapsulate creation to avoid that.
Common misconception
Thinking a single helper function fixes coupling. A simple factory centralizes branching but doesn't delegate creation via inheritance like Factory Method.
Key takeaway
Move constructors behind a factory interface so clients depend on abstract products, not concrete classes.
Analogy
Ordering from a menu
Imagine a client requests a "coffee" from an interface. The barista decides the concrete beans and brewing method. The client doesn't need to know the details. Factories play the barista role for objects.
Check your understanding
  • Can you find an if-else that constructs different classes in your project?
  • Would introducing a factory reduce places to change when adding a variant?

screens.title: Factory Method: Intent and Structure
screens.narratorSegment: The Factory Method pattern defines an abstract creator that declares a factory method and lets subclasses provide concrete implementations. The key claim is this: move the knowledge of which concrete product to instantiate out of the client and into subclasses of the creator. Structure-wise, you have an Abstract Product interface, Concrete Products that implement it, an Abstract Creator that declares the factory method, and Concrete Creators that override it to return specific products. A concrete example from the chapter uses a UIFactory with create_button. WindowsUIFactory returns a WindowsButton; MacUIFactory returns a MacButton. The advantage is that client code can call a creator operation like display_dialog which internally uses the factory method to obtain a button; the client never references concrete product classes. A common misunderstanding is to treat the factory method as a static utility; that shifts creation but loses polymorphic extension. Another mistake is to conflate the factory method with simple factories that select products based on parameters. Factory Method uses inheritance and deferred implementation, enabling new product types via new subclasses without modifying client code. Takeaway: when you need subclasses to decide which variant to create, implement a factory method and keep clients dependent on abstractions. How would you refactor your UI code to use a factory method today?

keyIdea.title: Factory Method
keyIdea.text: Declare a factory method in a creator interface and let subclasses return concrete products, keeping clients unaware of concrete classes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Factory Method
Definition
Factory Method: intent and structure
Declare a creation method and defer the instantiation to subclasses. Use when subclasses should determine the concrete product.
Pattern parts
Abstract Product, Concrete Products, Abstract Creator, Concrete Creators that override the factory method.
Misconception
Don't substitute a static helper for true Factory Method; inheritance provides extensibility the static helper cannot.
Code Walkthrough
# Abstract Product
class Button:
    def render(self):
        raise NotImplementedError

# Concrete Products
class WindowsButton(Button):
    def render(self):
        return "Rendering a Windows button."

class MacButton(Button):
    def render(self):
        return "Rendering a Mac button."

# Abstract Creator
class UIFactory:
    def create_button(self):
        raise NotImplementedError

    def display_dialog(self):
        button = self.create_button()
        return f"Dialog with: {button.render()}"
The creator exposes display_dialog which uses the factory method. Concrete creators implement create_button to return platform-specific products.

screens.title: Implementing Factory Method — Step by Step
screens.narratorSegment: To implement Factory Method reliably, follow a clear sequence. Step one: define an abstract product interface that describes the operations clients need. Step two: implement concrete products that satisfy that interface. Step three: declare an abstract creator that includes a factory method for producing the product and any higher-level operations that use the product. Step four: implement concrete creators that override the factory method and return the appropriate concrete product. Step five: update the client to depend on the abstract creator and abstract product only. For a concrete example, the UIFactory declares create_button and display_dialog; WindowsUIFactory overrides create_button to return WindowsButton. A common error during implementation is leaking concrete types back into client code by returning concrete classes in public APIs. Ensure creators return abstract product types. Another pitfall is overusing inheritance: if your language supports composition and dependency injection, prefer passing a factory instance rather than subclassing when runtime selection is required. The implementation checklist helps you verify correctness: do clients refer only to abstract products, do concrete creators only override factory methods, and can you add a new product variant by adding a new creator without editing clients? These checks guide a safe refactor.

keyIdea.text: Define product interfaces, implement concrete products, declare an abstract creator, override factory methods in concrete creators, and keep clients dependent on abstractions.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Implementing Factory Method
Process Flow
Steps to implement
1. Define Product
Declare the abstract product interface used by clients.
2. Concrete Products
Implement each variant of the product interface.
3. Abstract Creator
Declare the factory method and higher-level operations that use it.
4. Concrete Creators
Override the factory method to return concrete products.
5. Client Update
Make clients depend on the creator and product abstractions only.
Concrete example
UIFactory declares create_button; WindowsUIFactory returns WindowsButton; application calls display_dialog and remains unaware of concrete button types.
Common mistake
Returning concrete product types from public APIs or leaking constructors into clients undermines the pattern.
Check
Can you add a new creator subclass for a new variant without changing any client files?

screens.title: Factory Method vs Simple Factory
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing Factory Method with a simple factory helps clarify the design choices. A simple factory is typically a static or centralized function that returns different concrete products based on input parameters. It centralizes branching, which is helpful, but clients still depend on the simple factory and adding behavior often requires modifying that single function. Factory Method, by contrast, delegates creation to subclasses and uses polymorphism: concrete creators override a factory method to specify the product. The practical consequence is that Factory Method supports extension by adding new creator subclasses without modifying existing creators or clients. A common situation is choosing between the two when runtime selection is needed. If the selection is dynamic at runtime and you cannot pick or register a creator instance, a simple factory might be simpler. If your design can use subclassing to encapsulate creation and you care about extensibility via new variants, prefer Factory Method. Concrete example: a simple factory that takes a platform name and returns a button class centralizes conditionals; changing the factory affects all consumers. Factory Method moves that decision into concrete factory subclasses, protecting clients. Misconception: thinking Factory Method is always superior; it trades central control for extensibility through subclassing. Decide based on whether you need polymorphic creation or centralized selection.

keyIdea.text: Simple factory centralizes branching; Factory Method delegates creation to subclasses and supports extensibility without changing existing client code.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Factory Method vs Simple Factory
Comparison
Two approaches to creation
Simple Factory
A central helper that returns different products based on input parameters. Easy to implement but requires edits in the factory to add variants.
Factory Method
A creator class declares a factory method and leaves instantiation to subclasses, enabling extension via new creator subclasses without changing clients.
Decision guide
Prefer Factory Method for extensibility via inheritance. Use a simple factory for simple, centralized selection when runtime configuration drives choices and you accept modifying one helper when variants change.
Concrete scenario
If you have multiple platforms and expect new platforms over time, implement Factory Method so each platform has its own factory subclass. If you have a small, fixed set and prefer a single switch, a simple factory can be pragmatic.
Misconception
Mistaking a simple factory for Factory Method. They solve similar problems but with different extensibility models.
Check
Can adding a new variant be done by adding a subclass without changing existing creators? If yes, Factory Method fits.

screens.title: Extensibility and the Open/Closed Principle
screens.narratorSegment: Factory Method supports the Open/Closed Principle by making it possible to add new concrete products without modifying client code. The creator declares the factory method; adding a new variant is a matter of adding a new concrete creator that implements that method. For example, if your UIFactory system initially supports Windows and Mac, and later you need LinuxButton, you implement LinuxUIFactory that returns LinuxButton. Clients that depend on UIFactory or its abstract operations remain untouched. That said, a common trap is assuming that Factory Method removes all change costs: adding a new kind of product operation and its methods may still require changes to creators or product interfaces. In other words, Factory Method makes product variant extension straightforward, but extending product types across families may still require modifications. Another practical pitfall is forgetting to keep return types abstract; if a factory method signature exposes a concrete product class, clients become coupled again. As a rule, always program to interfaces and keep factory method signatures returning abstract product types. Final check: can you add a platform factory and register it at runtime without patching client logic? If yes, your design adheres to Open/Closed in practice.

keyIdea.title: Extensibility
keyIdea.text: Factory Method lets you add new concrete variants by introducing new creator subclasses, helping satisfy the Open/Closed Principle when clients use abstractions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Extensibility & O/C
Core Concept
Open/Closed and Factory Method
Add new variants via new creator subclasses; keep client code closed to modification by programming to abstractions.
Concrete example
Introduce LinuxUIFactory that returns LinuxButton; clients calling UIFactory operations remain unchanged.
Pitfall
Exposing concrete return types in factory signatures or leaking constructors into clients undoes the benefit.
Practical check
Can you add a new factory subclass without editing client code? If yes, the pattern protects your design.
Reflective question
Which class in your codebase currently violates Open/Closed because it constructs variants directly?
Analogy
Think of adding new menu items at a restaurant. If orders ask for a "sandwich" and the kitchen decides the filling, new fillings don't require changing the ordering interface.

screens.title: Abstract Factory: Families of Related Products
screens.narratorSegment: The Abstract Factory pattern extends the idea of encapsulated creation to families of products. Its intent is to provide an interface for creating related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes. Instead of a single factory method for one product, an abstract factory declares methods for creating each product in the family — for example, create_button and create_checkbox. Concrete factories implement those methods to return products specific to a family: WindowsGUIFactory produces WindowsButton and WindowsCheckbox; MacGUIFactory produces MacButton and MacCheckbox. This guarantees that products created by a concrete factory are compatible and consistent. A clear trade-off is that adding a new product type to the family (say a text field) requires updating the abstract factory interface and every concrete factory, which is more invasive. A common error is to add product types frequently; in that case Abstract Factory becomes costly to maintain. Use Abstract Factory when product families must be consistent across a client or when you need to switch entire families at once. Example: switching the UI theme from Windows to Mac involves passing a different factory; client code still only interacts with abstract product interfaces. Takeaway: Abstract Factory ensures product compatibility at the cost of making the factory interface more rigid when adding new product types.

keyIdea.title: Abstract Factory
keyIdea.text: Provide an interface to create families of related products so clients receive compatible components without knowing concrete classes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Abstract Factory
Definition
Abstract Factory: product families
An abstract factory declares creation methods for each product in a family. Concrete factories return matching product instances for that family.
Concrete example
GUIFactory with create_button and create_checkbox; WindowsGUIFactory returns WindowsButton and WindowsCheckbox ensuring compatibility.
Trade-off
Easy to add new families, harder to add new product types because the abstract factory interface must change and all concrete factories must be updated.
Check
If switching theme requires replacing multiple component types at once, Abstract Factory is a good fit. If you add product types often, reconsider.

screens.title: Abstract Factory in Code
screens.narratorSegment: This code walkthrough shows the Abstract Factory structure with two product types: Button and Checkbox. The abstract products declare operations: render for Button and paint for Checkbox. Concrete products implement those operations for each platform. The Abstract Factory declares methods create_button and create_checkbox. Concrete factories like WindowsGUIFactory return the Windows variants for both products. The client obtains a factory, requests each product, and uses their operations. For example, client_application calls factory. create_button and factory. create_checkbox and prints their output, demonstrating that both products come from the same family. A concrete advantage is guaranteed compatibility: components created by a given factory are designed to work together. A common misconception is to think Abstract Factory avoids all changes — adding a new product type requires changing the abstract factory and all concrete factories. Use Abstract Factory where product families are stable and must remain consistent. Try mentally adding a text field product: you would update GUIFactory and implement the new method in all concrete factories. That cost is the pattern's trade-off. Takeaway: Abstract Factory centralizes family creation and preserves cross-product consistency at the expense of adding work for new product types.

Code Walkthrough
GUIFactory with multiple products
# Abstract Product A
class Button:
    def render(self):
        raise NotImplementedError

# Concrete A
class WindowsButton(Button):
    def render(self):
        return "Rendering a Windows button."

class MacButton(Button):
    def render(self):
        return "Rendering a Mac button."

# Abstract Product B
class Checkbox:
    def paint(self):
        raise NotImplementedError

# Concrete B
class WindowsCheckbox(Checkbox):
    def paint(self):
        return "Painting a Windows checkbox."

class MacCheckbox(Checkbox):
    def paint(self):
        return "Painting a Mac checkbox."

# Abstract Factory
class GUIFactory:
    def create_button(self) -> Button:
        raise NotImplementedError
    def create_checkbox(self) -> Checkbox:
        raise NotImplementedError

WindowsGUIFactory returns WindowsButton and WindowsCheckbox; MacGUIFactory returns MacButton and MacCheckbox. The client uses only abstract interfaces.

Believing Abstract Factory removes all change costs. Adding new product types requires edits to the factory interface and all concrete factories.

screens.title: Implementing Abstract Factory — Patterns and Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: When implementing Abstract Factory, follow a disciplined process that surfaces trade-offs early. First, enumerate the product types that naturally belong together as a family — for example, button, checkbox, and possibly text field. Second, design abstract product interfaces for each type capturing only operations clients need. Third, declare an Abstract Factory interface that exposes a creation method for each product type. Fourth, implement concrete factories that return concrete product sets that are compatible by family. Fifth, ensure client code consumes products only through abstract interfaces and receives a factory instance to create needed components. The crucial trade-off is maintenance when adding new product types: adding a new create method to the Abstract Factory requires updating all concrete factories. If you expect frequent additions to product types, Abstract Factory may be costly. A practical approach is to limit the factory interface to stable product types or to provide extension points via small adapters. A common pitfall is mixing unrelated products into a single family. Keep families cohesive. Final check: can you swap the entire set of products by providing a different concrete factory without altering client logic? If yes, you've achieved the intended decoupling.

Designing families and handling changes

Group product types that must remain compatible across a client.

screens.title: Choosing Between Factory Method and Abstract Factory
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting the right pattern depends on whether you need to vary a single product type or entire families of products. If your problem is to let subclasses decide which single product to create — for example, which Button variant to instantiate — Factory Method is a natural fit. It encapsulates creation per product and supports adding new variants by creating new concrete creators. If instead you need to create a set of related products that must be compatible — buttons, checkboxes, text fields that belong together — Abstract Factory fits because it produces a consistent family from one factory. Consider these practical trade-offs: Abstract Factory makes switching themes or platforms straightforward, but adding a new product type is invasive; Factory Method is lighter for single-product variation but does not directly solve family consistency. A common error is mixing the concerns: using Factory Method for some product types and then manually pairing products can lead to compatibility bugs. Use the following checklist: Are products in the family tightly coupled in usage? Use Abstract Factory. Do you just need different variants of one product type with frequent new variants? Use Factory Method. Final question to reflect on: does your client need a full compatible set at runtime, or only a single variant? That answer points you to the right pattern.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Document Converter Activity
Hands-on Activity
Factory Method in a document converter
# Product Interface
class Converter:
    def convert(self, content):
        raise NotImplementedError

# Concrete Products
class PdfConverter(Converter):
    def convert(self, content):
        return f"Converting '{content}' to PDF format."

class HtmlConverter(Converter):
    def convert(self, content):
        return f"Converting '{content}' to HTML format."

# Abstract Creator
class Document:
    def create_converter(self) -> Converter:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def process_document(self, content):
        converter = self.create_converter()
        return converter.convert(content)

# TODO: Implement TextDocument and ImageDocument
class TextDocument(Document):
    pass

class ImageDocument(Document):
    pass

# --- Test ---
if __name__ == "__main__":
    text_doc = TextDocument()
    print(text_doc.process_document("My important report"))

    image_doc = ImageDocument()
    print(image_doc.process_document("Vacation photo metadata"))
Implementation hint
TextDocument.create_converter should return PdfConverter(); ImageDocument.create_converter should return HtmlConverter().
Common error
Instantiating converters directly inside process_document instead of using the factory method breaks the pattern's intent.
Expected output
Converting 'My important report' to PDF format.\nConverting 'Vacation photo metadata' to HTML format.

screens.narratorSegment: Here are the compact ideas to carry forward. First, Factory Method defines a creator interface with a factory method that subclasses override to supply concrete products; use it when you need subclass-driven creation of a single product type. Second, Abstract Factory provides methods to create families of related products so the client receives matching components; use it when you must switch entire families at once. Third, apply the Open/Closed Principle: prefer factories when you want to add new variants without editing client code. Use these short checks when reviewing designs: can you add a new product variant by adding a creator subclass? Can you swap a whole product family by providing a different factory? If the answers are yes, your design matches the intended patterns. Reflect on a current project and pick which pattern would reduce construction coupling most effectively.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we explore two creational patterns that free client code from knowing how objects are created. You will learn why encapsulating creation matters, how the Factory Method lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate, and how the Abstract Factory groups related products into compatible families. To ground this, we'll use a cross-platform UI example — think buttons and checkboxes that must behave consistently on Windows or Mac — and a small hands-on document-conversion activity. This matters because hard-coded instantiation with branching logic tightly couples clients to concrete classes and violates the Open/Closed Principle. A simple if-else that returns different button classes becomes a maintenance burden as platforms or product types grow. Throughout the lesson you will see concrete code examples that show the abstract interfaces, concrete products, and factory classes. You'll also compare Factory Method to a simple factory and learn the trade-off: Factory Method favors extensibility via inheritance, while Abstract Factory favors consistent product families. By the end, you should be able to choose the right pattern for single-product creation or for families of related products, and implement a clean factory structure in your codebase. Reflect: which part of your recent project would benefit from hiding creation details behind a factory?

These objectives focus your practice on the problem and the two patterns that solve it. First, you will identify the core problem Creational Patterns address: decoupling object creation from client code so implementations can change without breaking clients. Second, you will explain the intent, structure, and application of the Factory Method pattern, including how a creator interface and concrete creators collaborate. Third, you will implement Factory Method in a small example, enabling different concrete products to be made by subclasses. Fourth, you will distinguish Factory Method from a simple factory, understanding that Factory Method uses inheritance to delegate creation and supports extensibility without modifying client code. Each objective includes a short practical mnemonic or micro-check to help you verify competency. For example, when you inspect client code, you should be able to point to a factory method and explain which subclass controls the concrete type. That skill lets you refactor an if-else chain into a factory structure safely. Keep these objectives in mind as we move into code and patterns; they map directly to the hands-on activity and assessment items that follow.

These objectives emphasize families of products and practical trade-offs. First, you will understand the Abstract Factory pattern: it provides an interface to create related products like buttons and checkboxes without specifying their concrete classes. Second, you will implement Abstract Factory so multiple product families remain consistent — for example, a Windows factory returns both a Windows button and a Windows checkbox that match visually and behaviorally. Third, you will learn when Abstract Factory is the right tool: choose it when you need product compatibility across a family rather than a single varied product. Fourth, you will practice the hands-on activity: finish the document converter starter code using Factory Method, verifying behavior for PDF and H T M L converters. Each card contains a micro-mnemonic to check your work: can you add a new platform family without changing client code? Can you add a new product type without updating many factories? These checks highlight the trade-offs and will guide your implementation and assessment work.

Creational patterns address a simple but pervasive problem: client code depends on concrete classes when it instantiates objects directly. When clients perform branching logic to choose which class to construct, any change to creation details or any new variant forces edits in many places. Encapsulating creation means moving instantiation behind an abstract interface so clients ask for a product and don't know, nor need to know, the concrete class. Concretely, imagine UI code that needs platform-specific buttons. If you scatter conditionals that say "if platform is Windows, new WindowsButton; else if Mac, new MacButton", every new platform or change to construction logic requires touching those conditionals. Encapsulate creation by introducing a creator with a factory method and concrete factories that return the platform-specific button. A common misconception is that encapsulating creation adds unnecessary indirection; in truth, the indirection is an investment in stability and extension. Another misconception is to confuse this with just moving conditionals into a single helper function; that simple factory centralizes branching but still couples the helper and consumers differently than Factory Method, which delegates creation to subclasses. Key takeaway: hide construction behind an abstract contract so client code depends only on interfaces, enabling new variants without editing clients. Ask yourself: when you add a new product in your codebase, do you have to change many client files?

The Factory Method pattern defines an abstract creator that declares a factory method and lets subclasses provide concrete implementations. The key claim is this: move the knowledge of which concrete product to instantiate out of the client and into subclasses of the creator. Structure-wise, you have an Abstract Product interface, Concrete Products that implement it, an Abstract Creator that declares the factory method, and Concrete Creators that override it to return specific products. A concrete example from the chapter uses a UIFactory with create_button. WindowsUIFactory returns a WindowsButton; MacUIFactory returns a MacButton. The advantage is that client code can call a creator operation like display_dialog which internally uses the factory method to obtain a button; the client never references concrete product classes. A common misunderstanding is to treat the factory method as a static utility; that shifts creation but loses polymorphic extension. Another mistake is to conflate the factory method with simple factories that select products based on parameters. Factory Method uses inheritance and deferred implementation, enabling new product types via new subclasses without modifying client code. Takeaway: when you need subclasses to decide which variant to create, implement a factory method and keep clients dependent on abstractions. How would you refactor your UI code to use a factory method today?

To implement Factory Method reliably, follow a clear sequence. Step one: define an abstract product interface that describes the operations clients need. Step two: implement concrete products that satisfy that interface. Step three: declare an abstract creator that includes a factory method for producing the product and any higher-level operations that use the product. Step four: implement concrete creators that override the factory method and return the appropriate concrete product. Step five: update the client to depend on the abstract creator and abstract product only. For a concrete example, the UIFactory declares create_button and display_dialog; WindowsUIFactory overrides create_button to return WindowsButton. A common error during implementation is leaking concrete types back into client code by returning concrete classes in public APIs. Ensure creators return abstract product types. Another pitfall is overusing inheritance: if your language supports composition and dependency injection, prefer passing a factory instance rather than subclassing when runtime selection is required. The implementation checklist helps you verify correctness: do clients refer only to abstract products, do concrete creators only override factory methods, and can you add a new product variant by adding a new creator without editing clients? These checks guide a safe refactor.

Comparing Factory Method with a simple factory helps clarify the design choices. A simple factory is typically a static or centralized function that returns different concrete products based on input parameters. It centralizes branching, which is helpful, but clients still depend on the simple factory and adding behavior often requires modifying that single function. Factory Method, by contrast, delegates creation to subclasses and uses polymorphism: concrete creators override a factory method to specify the product. The practical consequence is that Factory Method supports extension by adding new creator subclasses without modifying existing creators or clients. A common situation is choosing between the two when runtime selection is needed. If the selection is dynamic at runtime and you cannot pick or register a creator instance, a simple factory might be simpler. If your design can use subclassing to encapsulate creation and you care about extensibility via new variants, prefer Factory Method. Concrete example: a simple factory that takes a platform name and returns a button class centralizes conditionals; changing the factory affects all consumers. Factory Method moves that decision into concrete factory subclasses, protecting clients. Misconception: thinking Factory Method is always superior; it trades central control for extensibility through subclassing. Decide based on whether you need polymorphic creation or centralized selection.

Factory Method supports the Open/Closed Principle by making it possible to add new concrete products without modifying client code. The creator declares the factory method; adding a new variant is a matter of adding a new concrete creator that implements that method. For example, if your UIFactory system initially supports Windows and Mac, and later you need LinuxButton, you implement LinuxUIFactory that returns LinuxButton. Clients that depend on UIFactory or its abstract operations remain untouched. That said, a common trap is assuming that Factory Method removes all change costs: adding a new kind of product operation and its methods may still require changes to creators or product interfaces. In other words, Factory Method makes product variant extension straightforward, but extending product types across families may still require modifications. Another practical pitfall is forgetting to keep return types abstract; if a factory method signature exposes a concrete product class, clients become coupled again. As a rule, always program to interfaces and keep factory method signatures returning abstract product types. Final check: can you add a platform factory and register it at runtime without patching client logic? If yes, your design adheres to Open/Closed in practice.

The Abstract Factory pattern extends the idea of encapsulated creation to families of products. Its intent is to provide an interface for creating related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes. Instead of a single factory method for one product, an abstract factory declares methods for creating each product in the family — for example, create_button and create_checkbox. Concrete factories implement those methods to return products specific to a family: WindowsGUIFactory produces WindowsButton and WindowsCheckbox; MacGUIFactory produces MacButton and MacCheckbox. This guarantees that products created by a concrete factory are compatible and consistent. A clear trade-off is that adding a new product type to the family (say a text field) requires updating the abstract factory interface and every concrete factory, which is more invasive. A common error is to add product types frequently; in that case Abstract Factory becomes costly to maintain. Use Abstract Factory when product families must be consistent across a client or when you need to switch entire families at once. Example: switching the UI theme from Windows to Mac involves passing a different factory; client code still only interacts with abstract product interfaces. Takeaway: Abstract Factory ensures product compatibility at the cost of making the factory interface more rigid when adding new product types.

This code walkthrough shows the Abstract Factory structure with two product types: Button and Checkbox. The abstract products declare operations: render for Button and paint for Checkbox. Concrete products implement those operations for each platform. The Abstract Factory declares methods create_button and create_checkbox. Use Abstract Factory where product families are stable and must remain consistent.
